title: Life Skills & Responsibility
description: Practical independence: dressing and tidying, helping at home, simple cooking, time management, organisation, decision-making, planning, budgeting basics, and preparing for adult life. Builds confidence through real responsibility.

units.title: I Can Do It Myself!

lessons.title: Getting Dressed by Myself
objectives: Put on clothes in the right order
Try fastenings like buttons, zips and velcro
explanation: Getting dressed by yourself is a big step! Clothes go on in an order: underwear first, then trousers or skirt, then a top, then socks, then shoes.
Buttons, zips and velcro take practice. Start with big buttons and practise on a shirt lying on the table before trying it on.
If something is tricky, try again slowly, and it's okay to ask for a little help.

vocabulary.meaning: a small disc that fastens clothes
a fastener that slides up and down

examples: Socks before shoes!
Tops with the label at the back.

story.title: Kiko's Upside-Down Morning
story.text: Kiko wanted to dress without help and put shoes on first, then tried to pull socks over them! Everyone giggled — Kiko too. Tara drew a picture chart: underwear, trousers, top, socks, shoes. The next morning, Kiko followed it and walked out proudly, all by myself!

activities.prompt: If something is tricky, you can…
options: try again slowly or ask for help

thinking: Which fastening is the hardest for you?
How do you feel when you do something by yourself?
speaking: Tell a grown-up the order you put your clothes on.

project.title: Dressing Picture Chart
steps: Draw each clothing item in order
Stick the chart near your clothes
Follow it every morning for a week
Add a sticker each day you dress by yourself

assessment.prompt: Asking for a little help is okay.

units.title: Tidy Up and Help Out
objectives: Tidy toys into the right places
Do a small helping job at home

revision.notes: Revisit through play: replay one activity, retell the story, and do one hands-on task. Keep revision under 5 minutes.

lessons.title: Tidy-Up Time
objectives: Tidy toys into the right places
Do a small helping job at home
explanation: When everything has a home, it's easy to find. Blocks go in the block box, books on the shelf, crayons in the crayon tin.
Tidying after play is part of being a good helper. A tidy-up song makes it fun!
You can help at home in other ways: setting spoons on the table, watering plants, putting socks in pairs, and feeding a pet with a grown-up.

vocabulary.meaning: put things back where they belong

examples: Matching socks into pairs.
Putting all the toy cars in one box.

story.title: The Missing Puzzle Piece
story.text: Momo couldn't finish a puzzle because one piece was missing. After searching everywhere, Momo found it under a pile of toys. "If everything had a home," said Mama Bear, "it would be easy to find." So Momo made labels for each box — and never lost a puzzle piece again.

activities.prompt: A helping job you can do:
Tidying helps us find things easily.
Match the item to its home

thinking: Why is it easier to play when your room is tidy?
What jobs do grown-ups in your home do every day?
speaking: Show a grown-up how you tidied your toys and where each thing lives.

project.title: Toy Home Labels
steps: Draw a picture label for each toy box
Stick labels on the boxes
Tidy all toys into the right boxes
Time yourself with a tidy-up song

assessment.prompt: Pairs of socks: 🧦🧦 🧦🧦 🧦🧦 — how many pairs?
Helping at home is part of being a family.

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: Ready for the Day
objectives: Follow a morning routine with a picture schedule
Explain why routines help
explanation: A routine is a set of things we do in the same order every day. A morning routine might be: wake up, use the toilet, brush teeth, wash face, get dressed, eat breakfast, pack bag.
Routines help us remember what to do, save time and feel calm because we know what comes next.
A picture schedule shows each step. Tick each one as you finish it.

vocabulary.meaning: things done in the same order every day
a plan showing when things happen

examples: Evening routine: bath, pyjamas, story, brush teeth, sleep.
Packing your school bag the night before.

story.title: The Rushed Morning
story.text: One morning Zuri overslept, couldn't find her shoes, forgot her water bottle and was late. That evening, she made a picture schedule and packed her bag before bed. The next morning, she followed the pictures, step by step, and had time for an extra cuddle before school.

activities.prompt: Packing your bag the night before saves time.

thinking: What happens when you skip a step in your routine?
Which part of your day do you like best?
speaking: Tell a grown-up your evening routine in order.

project.title: Picture Schedule
steps: Draw each step of your morning routine on a strip
Stick it on the wall
Move a peg along as you finish each step
Try it for a week and see if mornings feel easier

assessment.prompt: Routines can make us feel calm.

options: things done in the same order every day

Follow kitchen safety rules

lessons.title: Making Fruit Chaat
objectives: Follow a simple recipe step by step
Follow kitchen safety rules
explanation: Cooking starts with safety: wash hands, ask a grown-up before using knives or anything hot, and use a child-safe knife for soft foods.

A recipe tells us what we need (ingredients) and what to do (steps). Fruit chaat: wash fruits, have a grown-up help cut them, put them in a bowl, sprinkle a little chaat masala or lemon juice, and mix.
Cleaning up is part of cooking: put peels in the wet-waste bin and wash your bowl.

vocabulary.meaning: a food item used in a recipe

examples: Banana, apple and papaya make a colourful chaat.
Spreading butter on bread with a blunt knife.

story.title: Rangi's Rainbow Chaat
story.text: Rangi wanted to make something for the family picnic. With Grandma watching, Rangi washed the fruits, peeled a banana and used a safe knife to slice it. Grandma cut the apple. Rangi added pomegranate seeds and a squeeze of lemon. "A rainbow in a bowl!" everyone cheered.

activities.prompt: Before using a sharp knife, you should…
Cleaning up is part of cooking.
A list of foods needed for a recipe is the…

thinking: Why should grown-ups help with knives and stoves?
What other simple snack could you make?
speaking: Explain your recipe to someone step by step.

project.title: Make and Share a Snack
steps: Choose a simple recipe
Gather ingredients
Make it with an adult supervising
Serve it to your family and clean up

lessons.title: My To-Do List
objectives: Make and use a to-do list
Estimate how long tasks take
explanation: A to-do list helps you remember what needs doing and lets you tick things off — which feels great!
Put important things first. Estimate how long each takes: reading 15 minutes, maths 20 minutes, tidying 10 minutes.
A timer can help you focus: work for 20 minutes, then take a 5-minute break. Planning time means there's still time left to play.

vocabulary.meaning: a list of tasks to complete

examples: Doing homework before playing outside.
Setting a timer for 20 minutes of reading.

story.title: The Very Busy Saturday
story.text: Kiko wanted to play, help Grandma, finish a project and practise the flute — all on Saturday! Kiko wrote a list, numbered the most important first, and guessed how long each would take. By evening, everything was ticked off, and there was still time to play.

thinking: Why does time sometimes feel short or long?
What happens when we leave important things to the end?
speaking: Show someone your to-do list for tomorrow and explain the order.

project.title: Weekly Planner

Add homework and chores
Colour-code types of activity

units.title: Saving and Spending
objectives: Distinguish needs and wants
Make a plan to save for something

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: Save, Spend or Share?
objectives: Distinguish needs and wants
Make a plan to save for something
explanation: Needs are things we must have, like food, water, clothes and a home. Wants are nice to have, like toys and sweets.
Money can be spent, saved or shared. Saving means keeping money to buy something bigger later. Sharing means using some to help others.
Waiting to buy something you really want, instead of spending on small things now, is a powerful skill.
examples: Saving ₹10 a week for 10 weeks to buy a ₹100 book.
Sharing pocket money with a charity drive.

story.title: The Three Jars
story.text: Grandpa gave Zuri three jars labelled SAVE, SPEND and SHARE. Each time she got pocket money, she split it between them. After two months, her SAVE jar bought the paint set she wanted, her SHARE jar bought food for the animal shelter, and her SPEND jar had paid for a few treats along the way.

pairs: need, to stay warm and covered

activities.prompt: Save ₹10 a week. How many weeks to save ₹50?

thinking: Is it always easy to tell a need from a want?
How does it feel to wait and save for something?
speaking: Tell a grown-up something you would save for and how you would do it.

project.title: Save–Spend–Share Jars

Decide how to split any pocket money or play money

Celebrate when you reach it

assessment.prompt: Waiting to buy can help you get something you really want.

lessons.title: Decision Steps
objectives: Use a step-by-step process to make decisions
Weigh pros and cons of options
explanation: Good decisions follow steps: identify the decision, list options, think about consequences (good and bad) for each, choose, then review how it went.
A pros-and-cons list helps compare options. Some pros or cons matter more than others — think about your values and the people affected.
Decisions are influenced by feelings, friends, adverts and habits. Pausing helps you notice these influences.
examples: Choosing between football club and art club.
Deciding how to spend a birthday gift of money.

story.title: The Club Choice
story.text: Arjun could join only one club: football or coding. He listed pros and cons. Football: friends, exercise, but late evenings. Coding: he loved puzzles, but none of his friends were joining. He chose coding, then reviewed after a month. He'd made new friends and loved it.

thinking: Can a good decision still turn out badly? Why?
How do friends influence your decisions?
speaking: Talk someone through a real decision using the steps.

project.title: Decision Journal
steps: Record three real decisions over two weeks
For each, write options, pros and cons, and your choice
Review the outcome later
Note what you learned

assessment.prompt: Pausing can help you notice influences.

lessons.title: Sew a Button and Cook a Meal
objectives: Sew on a button
Cook a simple dish safely with supervision
explanation: Sewing a button: thread a needle and knot the end, push the needle up through the fabric and a buttonhole, down through the opposite hole, repeat several times, then knot underneath.

Simple cooking with supervision builds independence: making chai, poha or a vegetable upma involves measuring, chopping, heating and timing. Learn stove safety: handles turned in, sleeves rolled up, never leave the stove unattended.
Other useful skills: sorting laundry, folding clothes, changing a bulb (with power off and an adult), and tightening a loose screw.

vocabulary.meaning: a thin pointed tool for sewing
an adult watching to keep you safe

examples: Making chai: water, tea leaves, milk, sugar, boiled and strained.
Folding T-shirts neatly into drawers.

story.title: The Loose Button
story.text: Before a school function, Kavya's shirt button fell off. Everyone was busy. She remembered what Grandma taught her: thread, knot, up and down, up and down, knot underneath. Five minutes later, the button was back. "I fixed it myself!" she told Grandma that evening.

items: thread the needle and knot it
push up through fabric and buttonhole
go down through the opposite hole

activities.prompt: Cooking should be supervised until you are experienced.
Match the skill to the tool

thinking: Why are practical skills useful even if you can pay someone else?
Which skill would you like to learn next?
speaking: Teach someone a household skill you have learned.

stages.overview: Personal finance, goal-setting and study organisation.

units.title: Budgeting
objectives: Create a simple personal budget
Distinguish fixed and variable expenses

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Making a Budget
objectives: Create a simple personal budget
Distinguish fixed and variable expenses
explanation: A budget is a plan for money: income (money coming in) and expenses (money going out). The goal is to spend less than you earn and save the difference.
Fixed expenses stay the same (like a bus pass); variable expenses change (like snacks). Tracking spending shows where money really goes.
Impulse buying — buying without planning — can drain savings. A useful rule: wait 24 hours before buying non-essential items.

vocabulary.meaning: a cost that stays the same

examples: Monthly pocket money ₹500: bus ₹200 (fixed), snacks ₹150 (variable), save ₹150.
Waiting a day before buying a new gadget.

story.title: Where Did It Go?
story.text: Riya got ₹500 pocket money and had nothing left by the 15th. She tracked every rupee next month: ₹250 had gone on small snacks! She made a budget, set ₹150 aside for savings first, and by the end of term had saved enough for a book set she wanted.

activities.prompt: Waiting before buying can reduce impulse spending.

thinking: Why might "pay yourself first" (saving before spending) work well?
How do adverts encourage impulse buying?
speaking: Present your monthly budget to a parent and explain your choices.

project.title: One-Month Budget Challenge
steps: List your income for a month
Plan expenses and a savings goal
Track every expense
Compare plan vs actual and adjust

units.title: Setting and Reaching Goals
objectives: Write SMART goals
Plan milestones and track progress

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: SMART Goals
objectives: Write SMART goals
Plan milestones and track progress
explanation: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. "Get better at maths" is vague; "Complete 10 practice problems every weekday for 4 weeks to improve my test score" is SMART.
Break big goals into milestones — smaller steps with dates — and track progress on a chart.
Setbacks are normal. Review what happened, adjust the plan, and keep going.
examples: "Read 4 books by the end of the month."
"Run 2 km without stopping by 1 March."

story.title: The Swimming Goal
story.text: Ravi wanted to "learn swimming". His coach helped him write a SMART goal: "Swim 25 m without stopping by the end of the summer holidays, practising three times a week." He set milestones: float, kick, 5 m, 10 m. He missed one week when he was ill, adjusted, and reached 25 m with a week to spare.

activities.prompt: Setbacks are a normal part of reaching goals.

options: a smaller step towards a goal

thinking: Why do vague goals often fail?
How do you stay motivated over a long goal?
speaking: Share a SMART goal with someone and ask them to check in with you.

project.title: Goal Tracker
steps: Write one SMART goal
List 4–5 milestones with dates
Track progress weekly
Reflect at the end on what helped and what to change

units.title: Exploring Careers
objectives: Assess personal interests, strengths and values
Research career pathways and requirements

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Finding Your Path
objectives: Assess personal interests, strengths and values
Research career pathways and requirements
explanation: Choosing a career starts with knowing yourself: what you enjoy (interests), what you're good at (strengths), and what matters to you (values, like helping others or creativity).

Careers can be grouped into clusters: health, engineering and technology, arts and design, business, education, law, agriculture, skilled trades and more. Each has different education pathways — university degrees, diplomas, apprenticeships and vocational training.

Talking to people in a career (informational interviews), job shadowing, and internships help you learn what work is really like. Careers often change over a lifetime, so learning to learn matters most.

vocabulary.meaning: a path of work over time
education for a specific trade or skill
a conversation to learn about someone's job

examples: An ITI course leading to an electrician's career.
Interviewing a nurse about her daily work.

story.title: The Unexpected Path
story.text: Meera thought she wanted to be a doctor. After shadowing at a clinic, she realised what she loved most was explaining things to patients. She explored and found public health communication — combining science, writing and helping people. "Knowing myself mattered more than picking a famous job," she said.

options: a conversation to learn about someone's job

activities.prompt: Careers often change over a lifetime.

thinking: What would you do if you couldn't fail?
How might technology change jobs by the time you start working?
speaking: Conduct and present an informational interview with someone in a career that interests you.

project.title: Career Exploration Portfolio
steps: Complete an interests–strengths–values reflection
Research three careers (tasks, education, pay range, future demand)
Interview one professional
Write a plan for the next two years

units.title: Financial Literacy
objectives: Calculate simple and compound interest
Recognise and avoid common financial scams

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Interest, Credit and Scams
objectives: Calculate simple and compound interest
Recognise and avoid common financial scams
explanation: Banks pay interest on savings and charge interest on loans. Simple interest is calculated on the original amount; compound interest is calculated on the amount plus interest already added, so it grows faster over time — "interest on interest".
Credit (borrowing) can be useful but costly: high interest debt (like unpaid credit card balances) grows quickly. Borrow only what you can repay.

Scams try to trick people: never share OTPs, PINs or passwords; banks never ask for them by phone. Be suspicious of offers that sound too good to be true, urgent threats, and unknown links. In India, cyber fraud can be reported at the national helpline 1930.

context.text: India's national cybercrime helpline 1930 and the cybercrime.gov.in portal are used to report online financial fraud.

vocabulary.meaning: money paid for using or lending money
interest calculated on principal plus earlier interest
one-time password used to confirm transactions

examples: ₹1,000 at 10% simple interest for 2 years → ₹200 interest.
At 10% compound annually for 2 years → ₹210 interest.

story.title: The Urgent Call
story.text: Riya's grandfather got a call: "Your bank account will be blocked today! Share the OTP to verify." He nearly did, but remembered Riya's advice: banks never ask for OTPs. He hung up and called his bank directly. It was a scam. Riya helped him report it to 1930.

activities.prompt: ₹2,000 at 5% simple interest for 3 years. Interest?
Banks never ask for your OTP over the phone.

thinking: Why does starting to save early matter so much with compound interest?
Why do scams work even on smart people?
speaking: Teach an elderly relative three rules for avoiding phone and online scams.

project.title: Compound Interest Explorer
steps: Calculate savings of ₹1,000 a year at 7% compound interest over 10, 20 and 40 years

Graph the results
Write a short guide on scams and safe banking for your family
